text.p: Oil prices surged again on Friday on supply concerns. The copper price pulled out of its new nosedive to end just firmer in London while wheat eased.
The Commodities Research Bureau Index rose 1.57 to 247.79.
Copper business was erratic on the LME on Friday, with the market thrashing around either side of overnight closing levels before late covering ensured a higher close, traders said.

At one time the market seemed set for a smooth upward run, with a rise above $1,940 fostered by a 2,100-tonne warehouse stock fall. But recent uncertainty over direction was maintained, with liquidation this afternoon driving prices down to near $1,910 before the mini-rally on the late kerb.
"In reality, there is little sense or consistency in the market at the moment. It is getting pushed from pillar to post without much volume at times," one trader said.
Aluminium market sentiment was hurt by the recent break under $1,500, as well as today's 6,625-tonne inventory increase, and prices threatened to break down to $1,470 at one stage.
However, late end-week covering arrested the decline, and last trade was at $1,484, still down $8.

Nickel trading was whippy, with the market at one time threatening to break below $7,400 before late covering helped erase early losses. There was also talk of shipping problems from Norilsk, although this seems to be without foundation. Prices jumped above $7,500 during an excitable kerb, finishing the day at $7,520, up $20 a tonne.
Lead prices clawed away from a test of the $800 level, but still finished in the minus column. Last three months business was at $809.50, down $4.

Zinc came under technical pressure, with the market unable to hold above $1,040, and prices slid back into the old $1,030/1,040 band, despite a 2,775-tonne stock fall today. Last trade was at $1,034, down $6.

Tin took advantage of copper's kerb upturn to revert back towards the mid-$6,200 area the market has languished in for most of the week. A 525-tonne stock decline was also supportive, and prices closed at $6,240/50, up $20.

Gold eased slightly, with the market mood bearish after its failure to rally on U.S./Iraq tension. Bullion closed in London at $385.30/$385.80 vs $386.10/$386.60 on Thursday. In New York December futures on COMEX closed 80 cents down at $385.50.

CBOT wheat futures closed lower on indications of increasing supplies of wheat, slow exports and persistent reminders of keen competition. Wheat closed one to 5-1/4 cents per bushel lower, with September down one at $4.46-1/2 a bushel. Traders said Memphis-based analytical firm Sparks Companies Friday pegged 1996-97 U.S. wheat production at 2.333 billion bushels, above USDA's forecast in August for 2.249 billion. Also, there signs continue to point to increasing competition for U.S. wheat exports from the European Union, Australia and Canada.

NYMEX heating oil prices ended Friday with steep gains stoked by supply concerns in the United States and Europe, while October crude oil set a closing high partly on short covering. "The reason heating oil outperformed was on the legitimate concern that supplies are tight here and in Europe," said Tom Bentz, a trader with ING Derivatives. American Petroleum Institute's latest weekly data showed distillate stocks 14 percent below year ago, and traders expect upcoming diesel exports to further tighten supply. October crude oil settled 41 cents higher, marking a closing high of $23.85 a barrel. The contract high is $24.25 set Tuesday on the Iraqi conflict.

CSCE world sugar futures settled a thinly-traded session barely moved from opening levels, as prices relaxed after a volatile week of trade. The October contract climbed to an 18-month high of 12.20 earlier this week on mostly fund buying, which fueled prices out of a six-week trading range between 11.40-12.00 cents. October sugar, which expires September 30, closed 0.01 cent weaker at 12.00.
